title: The names
hook: Allah teaches Adam the names of all things, and the angels admit they know only what they were taught (2:31–33)
tomorrow: The one who would not bow

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalifah, the steward, and the angels' honest question. Your line was even the angels asked. What did you ask? Day twenty-three.

Think of a toddler pointing. Dog. Ball. Moon. Every new word is a small victory, and the whole family cheers. It seems so simple, but something enormous is happening: the world is splitting into things that can be told apart, held in the mind, talked about. Once a child can say moon, they can ask where it goes in the daytime. Yesterday, the angels asked why God would put this risky new creature on the earth, and God said: I know what you know not. Today, He shows them. And the answer, when it comes, isn't strength, or goodness. It's words.
screen: `A TODDLER POINTING: DOG, BALL, MOON.` → `THE WORLD SPLITS INTO THINGS.` → `THE ANSWER IS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse thirty-one. In Pickthall's words: “And He taught Adam all the names.” Then God sets the things before the angels and says, tell Me their names, if you're right. And the angels, who've been praising God since before there was a world, answer honestly: “We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us.” Then Adam is asked. And he names them, one by one. That's the answer to yesterday's question. What makes this creature worth the risk? He can be taught. He can learn names. What were the names? The Qur'an doesn't say, and the commentators have their favorite answers. Some early authorities said everything, down to a bowl and a cooking pot. Some said the names of the angels, or of Adam's own descendants. Many later thinkers read it as something bigger: the gift of language itself, the power to tell one thing from another and know it. A hadith in Bukhari, about the Day of Judgment, has people coming to Adam and reminding him of it: God taught you the names of all things. It was the first thing they remembered him for. And look at the angels. They don't pretend. They don't bluff. They say: we only know what we were taught. It's one of the most honest lines in the whole story, and it comes from creatures of light. To name a thing, you have to look at it long enough to tell it apart from everything else. Naming is noticing, made permanent.
screen: `HE TAUGHT ADAM ALL THE NAMES.` · `WE KNOW ONLY WHAT WE WERE TAUGHT.` · `WHAT WERE THE NAMES?` · `NAMING IS NOTICING.` · then, large: `TO NAME IS TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Open your eyes, and look slowly around the room. Name five things, silently, one at a time. Not quickly. Stay with each one until you've really seen it. The color of the mug. The way the light sits on the wall. The crack in the ceiling. The plant that needs water. Then close your eyes and name one thing you can hear, and one you can feel. If you pray, you can remember who, in the story, first taught the names. The bell holds the time.
The names. What God taught Adam, and what the angels didn't know: the first gift in the human story is words.
Your line: to name is to notice. Today, learn the name of one thing you pass every day and never knew: a tree, a bird, the person who makes your coffee. Day twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 23 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE WHO WOULD NOT BOW.`

howItsDone: Muslims often point to this passage as the root of Islam's regard for knowledge, and many teachers open lessons by recalling that God taught Adam the names.

original.note: Arabic: the names, plural of ism, name; in 2:31, al-asma'a kullaha, all the names.

trapdoor: what you thought: Adam made up names for the animals.
what it means: the names — God taught them to Adam, and he could say what the angels couldn't. being taught is what makes the steward worth the risk.
what a scholar hears: al-asma'a kullaha, all the names; early authorities said even a bowl and a pot; others read it as language, or the power to know things apart.

Bukhari 4476 (hadith of intercession) cited from memory; confirm.
